data.title: A writer for curious, connected readers.
data.intro: Freelance Writer is the working name of Rowan Blake, an independent writer and editor based in Bristol, writing about technology, work and the places we live in.

children.text: I write long-form articles, essays and clear, human copy for people who care how their ideas land. Most of my work begins with a conversation: what are you trying to say, and who needs to hear it?
How I work
I research carefully, write plainly and edit hard. You get a short plan before I start, a draft that is close to final, and one round of revisions included in every fixed quote.
I would rather turn down a piece I am not right for than deliver one that is merely fine. If I am not the best writer for the job, I will tell you, and usually know someone who is.
What I write about

Technology and its human side, productivity without the hype, and the way places and people shape one another. Selected work is on the Work page; the publications named there are fictional examples used to show how this theme looks with content.
Working together
Commissions open each quarter, usually four to six weeks ahead. Send a note through the contact page and I will reply with questions, a timeline and a fixed quote.

data.title: Usage and credits
data.intro: How the writing on this site may be shared.

children.text: All writing on this site is original and remains the property of its author. You are welcome to link to any article and to quote a short passage with a credit and a link back.
If you would like to republish a piece in full, reuse it in teaching materials or translate it, please get in touch first and we will agree terms in writing.

data.title: A Slower Internet Is a Kinder One
data.summary: Why a more mindful web can lead to happier, healthier lives.

children.text: Most of us did not choose the way we use the internet. It arrived in pieces: a feed here, a notification there, a reply that felt owed within the hour. Somewhere along the way, speed became the only thing anyone asked of it.
What speed took from us

A fast web rewards the quick reaction over the considered one. It trains us to skim, to forward, to answer before we have finished reading. The cost is rarely dramatic. It shows up as a low, constant tiredness, and as the sense that every conversation is happening at the wrong pace.

The people I spoke to for this piece had each, in their own way, slowed down: one moved her newsletters to a weekly digest, another publishes only when he has something to say. None of them described it as giving something up. They described getting something back.
Small rules, kinder habits

A slower internet does not need a manifesto. It needs a few small rules that are easy to keep: read before you reply, leave a day between a draft and a post, and treat a quiet inbox as a sign that things are working rather than a problem to be solved.
Kindness, it turns out, is mostly a matter of pace. Give people time and they tend to be generous.

data.title: The Power of a Focused Day
data.summary: Small changes that create bigger, brighter work.

children.text: A focused day rarely looks impressive from the outside. There is a cup of coffee, a notebook, and a list that is deliberately shorter than it could be.
Start with one sentence

Before opening anything else, write one sentence describing what would make the day a good one. Not a task list, a sentence. It is surprising how often the answer is a single piece of work that you have been circling for a week.
Protect the first two hours

Everyone has a window when their thinking is clearest. Mine is the morning, so email waits. The point is not discipline for its own sake, it is putting the hardest work where your attention is strongest.
By mid-afternoon the list is done, the day is quieter than it used to be, and the work is better for it.

data.title: What Places Teach Us
data.summary: Travel, perspective and the stories that shape a more open mind.

children.text: I used to think travel was about getting away. These days I think it is about paying a different kind of attention, the kind you give a place when nothing in it is yet familiar.
The slow arrival
The most useful journeys I have taken were the ones with room in them: a long walk between two villages, a train that was an hour late, a conversation that ran past the end of the afternoon.
Places teach in small, specific ways. How a town arranges its benches says something about how it expects people to meet. How a valley is farmed says something about what it has had to survive.
Bringing it home
The habit worth keeping is not the photographs. It is the willingness to look at your own street the way you looked at that valley, as if you had never seen it before.

data.title: The Case for a Quieter Desk
data.summary: What happens to your work when the room around it gets calmer.

children.text: A quiet desk is not an empty one. It is a desk where everything on it has a reason to be there, and where the thing you are working on is the loudest object in sight.
I keep a notebook, a pen and a cup. Everything else lives somewhere I have to stand up to reach. That small friction is the point: it makes every interruption a decision rather than a reflex.
The effect is hard to measure and easy to feel. Sentences come a little more slowly and land a little more cleanly. Drafts need fewer rounds.

data.title: Notes on Writing for a Living
data.summary: What a decade of commissions has taught me about listening first.

children.text: The job, it turns out, is mostly listening. A commission arrives as a topic and a word count, and the real work is finding the question underneath it that a reader would actually want answered.
Ask the second question
The first answer in an interview is usually the prepared one. The second, the follow-up that begins with 'what did that feel like', is where the piece tends to live.
I edit hard and I like being edited. A clear sentence is a courtesy to a stranger, and the strangers are the whole point.

data.title: Small Towns and Big Ideas
data.summary: Why some of the most interesting thinking happens far from the city.

children.text: There is a coastal town I keep returning to, partly for the light and partly for the people who run it, none of whom seem to be in a hurry and all of whom seem to be building something.
A library that doubles as a repair cafe. A harbour office that runs a reading group. Small places do not have the luxury of specialising, so their ideas tend to overlap in useful ways.
What big cities could learn from them is less about scale and more about attention: knowing your neighbours well enough to ask them for help.

data.title: How a Good Cup of Coffee Slows a Meeting
data.summary: A short essay on ritual, hospitality and the first five minutes.

children.text: The first five minutes of a meeting set the tone for the remaining fifty. A cup of something warm, handed over before anyone has asked a question, changes what the room expects of itself.
Ritual is not decoration. It tells people that there is time, and that the person across from them has been thought about before they arrived.
I have started every interview this way for years, and the answers are consistently better for it.

data.title: Better Questions, Brighter Ideas
data.summary: How the questions we ask our tools shape the ideas we end up with.

children.text: Every tool has a way of making some questions easy to ask and others invisible. Search taught us to ask for answers; a good book teaches us to ask for better questions.
In a month of interviews with teachers, editors and engineers, the same habit kept appearing: before reaching for the tool, they wrote down what they actually wanted to know.
It is a modest practice, and it has a way of changing everything downstream.
